What are the characteristics of living things?

Living things share seven characteristics, remembered with MRS GREN. Movement: living things move by themselves, even plants turning their leaves towards sunlight. Respiration: they release energy from food, which is why we breathe. Sensitivity: they respond to stimuli like light, heat and touch — think of how a mimosa plant folds when touched. Growth: they increase in size and complexity, as you have grown since primary school. Reproduction: they produce young ones of their own kind. Excretion: they remove waste products, like sweat and urine. Nutrition: they need food for energy and growth. Anything showing all seven is living; a goat, a mango tree and you all qualify, while a stone, a table and a bicycle show none of them.

What is the difference between living and non-living things?

Living things carry out all seven life processes (MRS GREN: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition), while non-living things carry out none of them. Living things are made of cells, need food, water and air, grow from within, and eventually die. Non-living things are not made of cells, do not feed or grow by themselves, and do not die because they were never alive. Examples of living things: humans, goats, fish, mango trees, grass, bacteria. Examples of non-living things: stones, chairs, water, air, sand, cars. Watch out for the tricky ones: a car moves and uses fuel but cannot grow or reproduce, so it is non-living; a seed looks lifeless but is living because it can germinate and grow.

Is a car a living thing? It moves and 'drinks' fuel.

Very clever thinking, but no — a car is a non-living thing. It is true that a car moves and consumes fuel, which makes it look alive at first glance. But apply the full MRS GREN test. Movement: yes, but only when a driver operates it, not by itself. Nutrition: it takes fuel, but it cannot make or digest food. Then the test fails completely: a car does not grow (a small car never becomes a big car), does not reproduce (two cars cannot produce a baby car), does not respond to stimuli on its own, does not excrete biological waste (exhaust fumes are combustion products, not excretion), and is not made of cells. A thing must show ALL seven characteristics to be living. This is exactly why scientists use a checklist rather than judging by appearance.

What is a cell and what are its main parts?

The cell is the smallest unit of life — the basic building block from which all living things are made, just as blocks build a house. Some organisms, like bacteria and amoeba, consist of only ONE cell and are called unicellular. Others, like humans, goats and trees, are made of billions of cells and are called multicellular. Every cell has three main parts: the cell membrane, a thin covering that controls what enters and leaves; the cytoplasm, the jelly-like fluid where activities happen; and the nucleus, the control centre that directs the cell. Plant cells have three extras that animal cells lack: a rigid cell wall, chloroplasts containing chlorophyll for photosynthesis, and a large vacuole. Cells are too small to see with the naked eye, so we use a microscope.

What is the difference between a plant cell and an animal cell?

Both cell types share a cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus and mitochondria, but plant cells have three structures that animal cells do not.

First, the cell WALL: a rigid layer of cellulose outside the membrane that gives the plant support and its fixed shape — this is why a plant stem stands upright without bones.
Second, CHLOROPLASTS: green structures containing chlorophyll, which trap sunlight for photosynthesis so plants make their own food.
Third, a large permanent VACUOLE filled with cell sap, which stores water and keeps the plant firm; when it loses water, the plant wilts, as you see with vegetables left in the sun. Animal cells have no wall (so they are flexible and round), no chloroplasts (so animals must eat food), and only small temporary vacuoles.

Explain the levels of organisation in living things

Living things are organised from the simplest level to the most complex, each level built from the one before it.

CELL: the basic unit of life, such as a red blood cell or a nerve cell.
TISSUE: a group of similar cells working together for one function, like muscle tissue or the xylem tissue in plants.
ORGAN: different tissues combined to perform a major function — the heart, the lungs, a leaf.
SYSTEM: several organs working together, like the digestive system (mouth, stomach, intestines) or the respiratory system.
ORGANISM: all the systems together forming one complete living being, such as a human, a goat or a maize plant. The chain runs: cells → tissues → organs → systems → organism. Learn it in order and you can answer any question on organisation levels.

Why is a seed considered living when it does not move or grow?

A seed is indeed living, even though it appears completely inactive. Inside every viable seed is a tiny living plant called the embryo, together with stored food, all wrapped in a protective seed coat. The seed is in a state called DORMANCY — its life processes have slowed almost to a stop so it can survive harsh conditions like the dry season or harmattan, sometimes for years. The proof that it is alive comes when you plant it: given water, warmth and air, the seed germinates and grows into a full plant. A dead seed, or one that has been boiled or is too old, will never germinate no matter how well you water it. Farmers test this by soaking seeds before planting: good seeds sink and sprout, dead ones float or rot. Dormant is not dead.

Give five examples each of living and non-living things in my school compound

Let us look around your school compound together. LIVING things: the mango or neem tree providing shade; the grass on the field; your classmates and teachers; the lizards running along the walls; and the ants, butterflies or birds moving about the compound. Each of these feeds, grows, responds to its surroundings and reproduces. NON-LIVING things: the classroom desks and chairs; the chalkboard; the school building and its blocks; the water in the tank or bucket; and the sand or stones on the ground. None of them feeds, grows or reproduces. Here is a good exercise for your notebook: draw two columns, walk around the compound at break time, and fill in ten items on each side — then test yourself by applying MRS GREN to any item a friend disputes.
